title: The Man Who Was Priced as the Company

Ten days ago the Nvidia board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation. This morning it reinstated him, unanimously, "with government input" according to Bloomberg, and the stock rose 30%. CNBC says that recovers nearly all of what it lost since the affair came out.

Sit with that for a second. The company's earnings last week were, in The Economist's words, roaring. Nothing about the chips, the customers, or the order book changed between Thursday and Monday. What changed is who sits in one chair. A $1 trillion-plus swing, driven by a personnel decision, then undone by another personnel decision. If you'd asked the market in October whether Nvidia was a company or a man, it would have said company, and then it spent a week proving otherwise with its own money.

I don't think this is irrational, exactly. Investors price key-person risk all the time, usually as a small discount. What's odd is that the discount turned out to be enormous in both directions, and that it took a scandal to reveal the size. The Times noted the board has a history of letting him get his way, which now reads less like a governance footnote and more like a description of what the asset actually was.

The broader tape is the other half of it. Reuters calls the morning "AI, caramba," Forbes argues the selloff looks like liquidation rather than repricing, and Asian authorities are propping up stocks. A $4 trillion wipeout followed by a one-stock bounce isn't a recovery so much as one very large position getting a reprieve. After six red days, people wanted a reason to buy, and a reinstated CEO is a cleaner story than "forced sellers ran out of things to sell."

Does anyone know yet which it was?
